nodes.title: Fixed 300s wall-clock budget makes step-count (throughput) the dominant lever on val_bpb, not per-step quality
nodes.rationale: TIME_BUDGET=300s is measured in wall-clock time (train.py: while True; break when total_training_time >= TIME_BUDGET), not fixed step count. With TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE=2**19 tokens/step and an ~8-layer/512-dim model, this experiment likely completes on the order of 1000-3000 optimizer steps -- deep in the undertrained regime. val_bpb = f(per-step quality) x (steps achieved in 300s). Anything that raises tok/sec directly buys more effective training and compounds across the whole run, unlike one-shot per-step quality changes.

nodes.title: Throughput/MFU headroom, not per-step quality, is the binding constraint at TIME_BUDGET=300s
nodes.rationale: TIME_BUDGET=300s is a hard wall-clock constant (prepare.py, comment: fixed, do not modify). val_bpb depends on (steps completed in 300s) x (quality per step). Champion model is small (depth=8, model_dim=512) on an H100 -- MFU is logged explicitly and is plausibly well below peak, meaning idle compute headroom exists. Throughput gains compound every experiment for the rest of the run; per-step quality gains are a one-time constant (HEARTBEAT structural-asymmetry rule).

nodes.title: Model depth/width geometry (ASPECT_RATIO=64, HEAD_DIM=128, DEPTH=8) was inherited from a longer-horizon speedrun recipe, not verified against this specific ~1-3k step budget
nodes.rationale: build_model_config derives model_dim=512, num_heads=4 from DEPTH=8 via a fixed ASPECT_RATIO. The optimizer (Muon/NorMuon), value-embedding ResFormer trick, and window pattern all read as lineage from nanochat/modded-nanogpt, tuned for a much longer training horizon. The compute-optimal depth/width split for a ~1-3k-step, 300s-wallclock budget is not obviously the same as for that longer budget, and DEPTH has apparently never been swept against this specific time budget.

nodes.title: Step-0 LR magnitude is miscalibrated for depth=8/dim=512 and unbuffered by warmup
nodes.rationale: setup_optimizer scales all AdamW LRs by dmodel_lr_scale=(model_dim/768)**-0.5, explicitly commented tuned at 768 dim. Champion model_dim=512 gives scale=1.2247 (22% LR boost vs the calibration point), applied at full strength from step 1 since WARMUP_RATIO=0.0. Muon momentum separately ramps over a hardcoded 300 steps (get_muon_momentum), independent of TIME_BUDGET, so if the whole run is only ~O(1000) steps, that ramp window is a large fraction of the run and overlaps with an unverified LR boost.

nodes.title: GPU compute is plausibly launch/overhead-bound rather than FLOPs-bound at this tiny model size, wasting wall-clock on overhead instead of matmuls
nodes.rationale: Non-embedding params are small (~25-30M) for n_layer=8, n_embd=512. DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE=128 gives grad_accum_steps=2 -- only 2 microsteps per optimizer step, so Python-loop/kernel-launch overhead is a larger fraction of step time than at higher device batch size. Separately, WINDOW_PATTERN=SSSL restricts 6 of 8 layers to half-context (1024 tok) attention, a FLOPs-saving trick that matters at large scale but for a model this small, attention FLOPs are likely a minor fraction of estimate_flops() next to the 4x-expansion MLPs -- windowing may be trading quality for negligible throughput here.

nodes.title: WARMDOWN_RATIO=0.5 is an untested constant inherited from a longer-horizon lineage
nodes.rationale: get_lr_multiplier spends the last 50% of counted training time decaying LR to FINAL_LR_FRAC=0.0. The file header states the script is cherry-picked and simplified from nanochat (a longer-horizon codebase); nothing in the code or logs indicates this fraction was re-derived for TIME_BUDGET=300s specifically. Whether half the (very short) counted budget should be spent in decay is untested.

nodes.title: Local shard cache confines every run to ~1.5-2.5 passes over a small corpus slice, so late-run tokens are increasingly repeats, not novel data
nodes.rationale: prepare.py --num-shards defaults to 10; the local cache at ~/.cache/autoresearch/data contains exactly 11 parquet files (10 train shards + the pinned val shard_06542), ~92MB each, ~920MB raw text total, out of climbmix-400b's 6542 available shards. The upstream README's own worked example of a 300s run on comparable hardware processed total_tokens_M=499.6. At ~4 bytes/token (vocab_size=8192), ~920MB of raw text is roughly 220-230M tokens, so a single experiment plausibly wraps the training shards 1.5-2.5x within its 300s budget (the epoch counter in prepare.py._document_batches literally increments on wraparound). This is fixed by how prepare.py was invoked at setup time (train.py cannot touch prepare.py or download more shards), so it is not a train.py lever by itself, but it changes how results should be read: (a) anti-memorization/regularization ideas may pay off more than a true-single-epoch reading of a 400B-token dataset would suggest, and (b) marginal tokens from any throughput-boosting idea are increasingly repeats past the first pass, not new signal.

nodes.title: Idle VRAM/FLOPs headroom (HEARTBEAT Step 1e) is unaudited and may be better spent on MORE CAPACITY, not just more steps
nodes.rationale: TASK.md/program.md explicitly say VRAM is a soft constraint ("some increase is acceptable for meaningful val_bpb gains"), and depth=8/dim=512 is small for an H100-class GPU. champion.md is still empty (round 0, no baseline logged yet in this workshop), so nobody has audited peak_vram_mb / mfu_percent against the 70%/50% thresholds HEARTBEAT Step 1e mandates. This is deliberately a different lever from D1/D1-throughput: D1-family proposals (bigger DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE, cheaper WINDOW_PATTERN) spend idle compute on MORE STEPS of the same tiny model; D5 spends the same idle compute on a BIGGER model at similar per-step wall time. Both draw on the same idle-headroom resource but through different mechanisms, so they are good candidates for independent (parallelizable) rather than alternative relations -- a result on one is evidence about whether headroom exists at all, but does not directly settle the other.

nodes.title: Model shape (DEPTH=8, ASPECT_RATIO=64, HEAD_DIM=128 -> n_embd=512, n_head=4) has no stated justification for being compute-optimal at a 300s wall-clock budget
nodes.rationale: ASPECT_RATIO, HEAD_DIM and DEPTH are hardcoded with no comment tying them to the 5-minute budget specifically, contrast with TIME_BUDGET itself, which prepare.py explicitly marks 'fixed, do not modify'. A shape that is compute-optimal for a much longer run is not necessarily optimal for a run this short: a shorter run amplifies the cost of any fixed per-step overhead (Python loop, kernel launch, compile) relative to matmul FLOPs, which can favor a different depth/width trade-off than a longer-run-tuned default.

nodes.title: The custom Python best-fit document-packing dataloader may be CPU-bound and starving the GPU
nodes.rationale: make_dataloader in prepare.py builds each training row with a per-row `while pos < row_capacity` loop that does a linear scan over up to `buffer_size=1000` buffered docs to find the best-fit doc, refilling via `tokenizer.encode` (CPU, num_threads=8) when the buffer runs low. This runs synchronously inside the training loop's micro-step: `for micro_step in range(grad_accum_steps): ... x, y, epoch = next(train_loader)` -- there is no separate prefetch thread/process, so CPU packing work and GPU compute are not obviously overlapped.

nodes.title: Muon momentum warmup is pinned to a fixed 300 raw steps, not rescaled to this run's actual (throughput-dependent) step count
nodes.rationale: get_muon_momentum(step): `frac = min(step/300, 1); return (1-frac)*0.85 + frac*0.95` ramps on raw step index. Every other schedule in the file (get_lr_multiplier, get_weight_decay) is driven by `progress = total_training_time/TIME_BUDGET`, i.e. by wall-clock fraction of the 300s budget, so those auto-rescale to however many steps this run actually gets. The momentum ramp does not: if the achieved step count for this run is anywhere near or below 300, the optimizer spends a large fraction of the whole run below its target 0.95 momentum. Cheap to confirm: the very first baseline run already prints num_steps in its final summary block -- no extra experiment needed just to check whether 300 is a large or small fraction of the achieved step count.

nodes.title: The wall-clock-fraction LR schedule (WARMUP_RATIO=0, WARMDOWN_RATIO=0.5) spends half the entire 300s budget cooling down, with no evidence it was tuned for this specific short budget
nodes.rationale: get_lr_multiplier spends the first 50% of progress at full LR (no warmup) and the last 50% ramping linearly to FINAL_LR_FRAC=0.0. For a budget this short, half of all optimizer steps happen during cooldown at a discounted LR -- a large fraction of an already-scarce step budget spent below peak. Whether 50% cooldown is too much, too little, or right is untested at this specific (5-minute) scale; the ratio reads like a default inherited from a differently-scaled base recipe.

nodes.title: Training is wall-clock-bound: optimizer-step count (and therefore everything downstream of it) is a pure function of tok/sec
nodes.rationale: prepare.py fixes TIME_BUDGET=300 (5 min) and train.py's main loop is `while True: ... if step>10 and total_training_time>=TIME_BUDGET: break` -- there is no target step or token count anywhere in the file. num_steps, and therefore how many LR/momentum/weight-decay schedule points and how many Muon/AdamW updates the model gets, is a pure function of tok/sec. Every change that raises tok/sec (bigger batch, cheaper compile, less CPU overhead) buys more optimizer steps for the *entire* remainder of training, while a change that only improves per-step loss quality is a one-time additive gain. Because the budget is wall-clock seconds rather than epochs or tokens, this asymmetry is unusually literal here.

nodes.title: anonymous write
probe diag schema
nodes.cut_reason: schema probe during round-0 setup, not a real diagnosis

nodes.title: Shrink WARMDOWN_RATIO from 0.5 to 0.2, spending more of the fixed ~1-3k step budget at peak LR
nodes.rationale: WARMDOWN_RATIO=0.5 reads as borrowed from a longer-horizon speedrun recipe. If D1 is right that this run is step-starved, spending half of a *tiny* step budget on LR decay (vs. a large step budget where 50% is still many thousands of high-LR steps) may be badly miscalibrated. Single-line change: WARMDOWN_RATIO = 0.2.
nodes.if_works: val_bpb improves -> confirms WARMDOWN_RATIO=0.5 was tuned for a different (longer) step-budget regime and is currently miscalibrated; other schedule constants borrowed from the same recipe (WARMUP_RATIO=0.0, the 300-step Muon momentum ramp in get_muon_momentum) should be re-audited against the actual ~1-3k step count next.
nodes.if_fails: Two distinguishable cases: (a) if final train loss is still falling steeply right up to the cutoff under the new schedule, 0.5 warmdown was genuinely needed even at this short horizon -- the schedule shape matters, not just average LR; (b) if train loss plateaus early either way and val_bpb is flat within noise, NorMuon+cautious weight decay likely makes this run insensitive to warmdown shape, meaning schedule-shape tuning is not where the leverage is and D1 should redirect toward raw throughput (I3/I4) instead of schedule shape.

nodes.title: Bracket DEPTH in {6, 10} vs baseline 8 at fixed ASPECT_RATIO/HEAD_DIM, same 300s budget
nodes.rationale: DEPTH=8 is the only value ever tried. Depth trades capacity-per-step against steps-achieved-per-second (deeper=more FLOPs/token=fewer steps in 300s; shallower=fewer FLOPs/token=more steps). Bracketing on both sides of 8 tells us whether the current depth is near the compute-optimal point for this specific token budget or whether the whole model-size axis has been sitting untested.
nodes.if_works: If DEPTH=6 or DEPTH=10 strictly beats DEPTH=8, the compute-optimal depth for this budget differs from the hand-picked default -- re-run ASPECT_RATIO/HEAD_DIM sweeps around the new optimum, since those were only ever tuned relative to depth=8.
nodes.if_fails: If both DEPTH=6 and DEPTH=10 are worse than DEPTH=8, that only closes the depth axis at fixed ASPECT_RATIO -- it does NOT validate ASPECT_RATIO=64 or HEAD_DIM=128 themselves, since a depth change at fixed aspect ratio confounds depth with model_dim/num_heads simultaneously. Would need a width-only sweep (fixed depth, varying ASPECT_RATIO) as the follow-up to actually isolate the width axis.

nodes.title: Raise DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 128->256 (grad_accum_steps 2->1) to cut per-optimizer-step Python/launch overhead and raise tok/sec
nodes.rationale: tokens_per_fwdbwd = DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE * MAX_SEQ_LEN; at 128 this gives grad_accum_steps=2, meaning every optimizer step pays kernel-launch and Python-loop overhead twice. If overhead is a meaningful fraction of step time for this tiny model (D3), doubling device batch size to remove one microstep of overhead per optimizer step should raise measured tok/sec and mfu_percent (both already printed by train.py), and more steps should fit in the fixed 300s. Needs a VRAM headroom check first (peak_vram_mb is already logged) since H100 80GB should have large headroom for a ~25-30M-param model at batch 128.
nodes.if_works: tok/sec and mfu_percent rise and val_bpb improves -> confirms D3 (this run is overhead/launch-bound, not FLOPs-bound) and that grad_accum_steps=2 specifically was a real tax; worth pushing DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE further (512?) until VRAM or diminishing returns bite.
nodes.if_fails: If tok/sec and mfu_percent do NOT rise, overhead is not concentrated in the grad-accum loop -- points blame elsewhere within D3 (e.g. the attention windowing in I4, or fixed per-step costs like the .item() sync and logging print on every step, which forces a host-device sync each iteration). If tok/sec rises but val_bpb does not improve, larger per-step batch is hurting sample efficiency enough to offset the extra steps -- a distinct, useful finding about batch-size/steps tradeoff at this scale.

nodes.title: Change WINDOW_PATTERN from SSSL to LLLL (full attention every layer) to test whether windowing buys real throughput at this tiny scale, or only costs quality
nodes.rationale: WINDOW_PATTERN=SSSL restricts 6/8 layers to half-context (1024 tok) attention -- a FLOPs-saving device that matters when attention FLOPs are a large share of the compute (long context / big models). At n_embd=512, MLP FLOPs (2x 4x-expansion matmuls) likely dwarf attention FLOPs even at full T=2048 context with FA3, so the throughput benefit of windowing may be small while the quality cost (losing half the context in most layers) is real.
nodes.if_works: val_bpb improves with LLLL and tok/sec drops only marginally (steps roughly unchanged) -> windowing was a bad quality/speed trade at this model size; adopt LLLL as default and stop treating window pattern as a free efficiency knob below some model-size threshold (worth then finding that threshold).
nodes.if_fails: If tok/sec drops materially and/or val_bpb does not improve enough to offset fewer steps achieved, windowing is genuinely buying throughput even here -- supports D3 as real but localizes the overhead specifically in attention compute/memory traffic rather than in launch overhead, distinguishing this from I3's result.

nodes.title: Prefetch the next batch on a background thread while the current micro-step's forward/backward runs, instead of a blocking next(train_loader) in the hot loop
nodes.rationale: Currently `x, y, epoch = next(train_loader)` for every micro_step is a blocking Python call inside the training loop, interleaved with loss.backward(). If the CPU-side packing work is non-trivial relative to one micro-step's GPU time, this serializes CPU and GPU work that could otherwise overlap.
nodes.if_works: tok/sec rises without touching the model/optimizer at all, and val_bpb improves purely from more steps fitting in 300s -- strong direct confirmation of D_dataloader as a real bottleneck, and implies the same overlap trick is worth applying to eval too.
nodes.if_fails: tok/sec is unchanged within noise -- this essentially rules out the dataloader as the bottleneck (CPU packing was already fully hidden behind GPU compute), which should raise confidence in the small-matmul/compute-bound reading of D_throughput and lower priority on further dataloader work.

nodes.title: Raise DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE (128 -> ~192-256) to amortize per-micro-step overhead over more tokens
nodes.rationale: grad_accum_steps = TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE/(DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE*MAX_SEQ_LEN) = 2 currently; every micro-step pays a fixed CPU/dataloader/dispatch overhead regardless of DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE, so a larger device batch spreads that fixed cost over more useful GPU work per micro-step, raising tok/sec if we are not yet VRAM-bound.
nodes.if_works: tok/sec and mfu% (printed every step) rise measurably and val_bpb strictly improves over champion; confirms D_throughput (steps are the scarce resource) AND that fixed per-micro-step overhead -- not raw matmul compute -- is currently eating into it, which makes I_compile_mode and I_async_loader worth trying even harder since they attack the same overhead from other angles.
nodes.if_fails: either OOM (need a smaller bump or grad checkpointing -- points at a VRAM-bound sub-issue we have not stated yet) or tok/sec is essentially unchanged, which rules out per-micro-step Python overhead as the bottleneck and redirects attention to raw compute (small-matmul MFU ceiling) or the dataloader itself -- makes D_dataloader more likely, not less.

nodes.title: Try torch.compile(model, mode='reduce-overhead') or 'max-autotune' instead of the current default mode
nodes.rationale: `model = torch.compile(model, dynamic=False)` uses the default compile mode. reduce-overhead uses CUDA graphs to cut Python/launch overhead per step; max-autotune spends more compile time searching for faster kernels. Either could raise steady-state tok/sec at the cost of a longer one-time compile phase, which does not count against TIME_BUDGET since total_training_time only accumulates after step>10.
nodes.if_works: steady-state tok/sec (post step 10) rises and val_bpb improves over champion; supports D_throughput and specifically implicates kernel-dispatch/launch overhead (not the dataloader) as a limiting mechanism.
nodes.if_fails: no meaningful tok/sec change, or compile errors/fails to capture a graph (the packing dataloader has data-dependent shapes) -- an error is itself informative: it would mean the dataloader's control flow is incompatible with more aggressive compilation, a concrete argument for decoupling data prep from the compiled step (relevant to D_dataloader).

nodes.title: Sweep model shape (e.g. DEPTH=6 with larger ASPECT_RATIO, or DEPTH=12 with smaller ASPECT_RATIO) to check whether DEPTH=8/dim=512 is compute-optimal for a 300s run
nodes.rationale: num_flops_per_token and tok/sec both depend on model shape, and TIME_BUDGET is wall-clock (not token) fixed, so the compute-optimal shape at this specific short budget could differ from whatever DEPTH=8 was tuned against. Each trial is a single-constant change and a full but cheap (5-minute) run.
nodes.if_works: val_bpb improves over champion with a different DEPTH/ASPECT_RATIO combination -- confirms D_capacity and opens a real architecture-search axis worth a proper depth x width grid, not just one point.
nodes.if_fails: val_bpb is worse or flat across shapes tried -- suggests DEPTH=8 (or nearby) is already close to a local optimum for this budget, so further capacity-shape search is low value and effort should concentrate on D_throughput/D_dataloader/D_muon_ramp instead.

nodes.title: Rescale the Muon momentum warmup from a fixed 300 raw steps to a much smaller constant (e.g. 50 steps)
nodes.rationale: get_muon_momentum uses frac=min(step/300,1). If the baseline run's printed num_steps ends up in the low hundreds, most/all of training happens with momentum below its 0.95 target. Shortening the ramp reaches target momentum much earlier in a short run without meaningfully changing a longer run.
nodes.if_works: val_bpb improves over champion, confirming D_muon_ramp: the momentum ramp constant was mismatched to this budget, and reaching target momentum earlier genuinely helps -- worth then trying to time-scale it like the other schedules instead of hardcoding a second constant.
nodes.if_fails: no improvement, or a regression (e.g. instability from high momentum before the model has 'warmed up') -- a regression argues momentum needs to ramp slowly regardless of run length (a genuine stability reason for 300, not just an unrescaled leftover), which kills D_muon_ramp as stated and redirects weight to D_throughput / D_dataloader instead.

nodes.title: Decrease WARMDOWN_RATIO (0.5 -> ~0.25) so more of the 300s budget runs at peak LR
nodes.rationale: Currently the last 50% of progress is spent linearly decaying LR to 0. Shortening cooldown trades final-LR polish for more high-LR optimization time, which may matter more when the total step budget is already small.
nodes.if_works: val_bpb improves over champion -- confirms the current 0.5 ratio wastes scarce steps in this very short regime, and is worth pushing further (e.g. 0.15-0.2) in a follow-up.
nodes.if_fails: val_bpb is worse -- means the cooldown is doing real consolidation work (final loss lands lower with it) even in a 300s run, which argues for trying the opposite direction instead (see I_warmdown_up).

nodes.title: Increase WARMDOWN_RATIO (0.5 -> ~0.7) so more of the run cools down at the cost of peak-LR time
nodes.rationale: Opposite-direction test on the same knob as I_warmdown_down; held at NEXT because running both directions before seeing either result wastes a NOW slot on a knob we can test one point at a time -- the graph should DEMOTE this the moment the other direction's result comes in as a clear win.
nodes.if_works: val_bpb improves over champion with more cooldown -- confirms the model benefits from a gentler wind-down even at the cost of high-LR time in this short regime.
nodes.if_fails: val_bpb is worse -- combined with I_warmdown_down's outcome this pins down whether 0.5 is already close to right (both directions worse) or whether the true optimum lies further from 0.5 in whichever direction won.

nodes.title: Set WARMUP_RATIO 0.0 -> 0.05 to buffer the step-0 full-strength, up-scaled LR
nodes.rationale: Champion applies full LR (already boosted 22% by dmodel_lr_scale for this smaller-than-768 model) from step 1 with zero warmup, while Muon momentum itself is still ramping over its first 300 (fixed) steps. A short linear warmup would separate whether early instability is wasting steps in this short-horizon regime.
nodes.if_works: val_bpb improves. Confirms early-step LR/momentum mismatch was real and costing training quality; motivates a follow-up warmup-fraction sweep and re-deriving dmodel_lr_scale for small dims specifically (not just assuming the 768-tuned power law holds).
nodes.if_fails: Distinguish by the early train_loss curve (first ~50-100 steps): if the curve is unchanged (no early spike either way), step-0 instability was never a real problem here and D2 is refuted in favor of D1/D3. If the early curve improves but final val_bpb is flat or worse, warmup ate steps at below-peak LR that were worth more as full-LR steps -- i.e. step count (D1) dominates stability (D2) at this budget.

nodes.title: Raise DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE 128 -> 256 (halve grad_accum_steps) to test compute headroom
nodes.rationale: If the H100 is underutilized at DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE=128 (low MFU), doubling it should raise tok/sec and MFU, giving more effective gradient signal per wall-clock second inside the fixed 300s budget without changing model quality per step.
nodes.if_works: val_bpb improves and logged mfu/tok_per_sec rise materially. Confirms D1: the run is throughput-bound, not quality-bound, and every future proposal should be screened for whether it also raises tok/sec -- architecture tweaks that cost tok/sec need a strong per-step argument to be worth proposing.
nodes.if_fails: Two distinguishable cases from the log: (a) OOM / peak_vram_mb spikes to the ceiling -> we were already near the memory ceiling, so headroom must come from elsewhere (shorter window, fewer KV heads) not raw batch size. (b) it runs fine, mfu/tok_per_sec rise, but val_bpb does not improve -> the model was already token-throughput-saturated for its capacity at this depth, which weakens D1 relative to D2/D3 and argues quality-per-step matters more than we assumed.
nodes.surprise_if: mfu/tok_per_sec DROP when batch size increases -- would mean something else (e.g. attention kernel scaling, dataloader stalls) is the real bottleneck, not raw batch/step size, and D1 needs to be rewritten around that mechanism instead.

nodes.title: Bypass dmodel_lr_scale: sweep MATRIX_LR/EMBEDDING_LR directly at dim=512 instead of trusting the 768-tuned 1/sqrt(dim) law
nodes.rationale: dmodel_lr_scale=(model_dim/768)**-0.5 is explicitly commented as tuned at 768 dim and applied uniformly regardless of depth/width. Nobody has verified this power law holds at model_dim=512 (current champion) rather than just being extrapolated. Directly probing LR values (e.g. -20%/+20% around the current auto-scaled value) at fixed dim=512 tells us whether the auto-scale formula is already near-optimal here or systematically off.
nodes.if_works: If a hand-tuned LR away from the auto-scaled value KEEPs, the 768-tuned power law is measurably wrong at this width, and the auto-scale formula itself becomes a standing axis to fix once (it silently affects every future depth-sweep experiment too).
nodes.if_fails: If no LR value in the probed range beats the current auto-scaled setting, the formula is already well-calibrated at this width, which strengthens confidence that D2 is not the binding constraint and future depth changes can keep trusting dmodel_lr_scale as-is.

nodes.title: Cut WARMDOWN_RATIO 0.5 -> 0.2 to spend more of the 300s budget at peak LR
nodes.rationale: get_lr_multiplier decays LR to 0 over the last WARMDOWN_RATIO fraction of counted training time. At WARMDOWN_RATIO=0.5, half of every short 300s run is spent below peak LR. Shrinking the decay fraction tests whether this value (apparently inherited from a longer-horizon codebase per the nanochat header comment) is too conservative for a 5-minute budget.
nodes.if_works: val_bpb improves. Confirms schedule fractions should scale with TIME_BUDGET rather than being fixed constants, and opens a systematic re-derivation of every ratio constant (WARMUP_RATIO, WARMDOWN_RATIO) specifically for TIME_BUDGET=300s.
nodes.if_fails: val_bpb gets worse or flat -> the final low-LR phase is doing real convergence/stabilization work even in a short run, i.e. quality of the last steps matters more than raw peak-LR step count, which argues against shrinking warmdown further and suggests the opposite direction (idea-warmdown-up) is more likely to help.

nodes.title: Raise WARMDOWN_RATIO 0.5 -> 0.7 to test the opposite direction on the same knob
nodes.rationale: Per the propose-both-directions rule: WARMDOWN_RATIO has only been examined in the decrease direction (idea-warmdown-down) so far. Testing the increase direction brackets the knob and tells us whether val_bpb responds monotonically to warmdown fraction at this budget, or whether 0.5 is already near a local optimum.
nodes.if_works: val_bpb improves with MORE decay time -> means the current champion has too little stabilization, which is the opposite conclusion from D3's original framing and would flip priority toward preserving/extending warmdown rather than cutting it.
nodes.if_fails: val_bpb gets worse or flat -> combined with idea-warmdown-down's result, this brackets a local optimum near WARMDOWN_RATIO=0.5 and the axis can be closed (report both deltas relative to noise floor before cutting).

nodes.title: Stop decaying weight_decay to 0 with progress -- hold WEIGHT_DECAY constant through training instead of get_weight_decay(progress)=WD*(1-progress)
nodes.rationale: get_weight_decay(progress) linearly decays Muon weight decay from WEIGHT_DECAY=0.2 to 0 over the run. If D4 is right that later training time is spent on repeated documents (2nd+ pass through the 10-shard cache), regularization pressure is being removed from the optimizer exactly when repeat-driven overfitting risk is highest. This is a single-line change: return WEIGHT_DECAY unconditionally instead of scaling by (1-progress).
nodes.if_works: val_bpb improves, meaning repeated-data overfitting in the back half of the run was a real and previously-untested cost -- other anti-repeat ideas (shuffling document order across passes, dropout, even higher WD) become worth prioritizing, and D4 graduates from a reading-caveat to an actionable diagnosis.
nodes.if_fails: val_bpb is flat or worse. Two sub-cases distinguishable from the training log: if train_loss near the back half stays smooth (no divergence/plateau from removed decay) but val_bpb does not improve, the model is still underfit even on repeated data at this budget (300s is not enough to memorize a ~230M-token corpus), so regularization is not yet binding and effort should stay on D1/D5 (throughput/capacity). If train_loss gets visibly worse late in the run (constant WD hurts optimization directly, independent of overfitting), that is evidence the progress-based WD decay is load-bearing for optimization dynamics, not just anti-overfitting -- keep it and look elsewhere.
nodes.surprise_if: val_bpb improves by a large margin -- would mean this run's data budget is far more repeat-bound than the back-of-envelope estimate in D4, and the shard-count constraint deserves escalating to the monitor/theorist as an infra fix (download more shards) rather than a train.py workaround.

nodes.title: Widen the model via ASPECT_RATIO 64->96 at fixed DEPTH=8 (model_dim 512->768) to spend idle VRAM/FLOPs headroom on capacity rather than step count
nodes.rationale: build_model_config derives model_dim purely from DEPTH*ASPECT_RATIO rounded to a HEAD_DIM multiple. Raising ASPECT_RATIO from 64 to 96 takes model_dim from 512 to 768 (num_heads 4->6) at the SAME depth, directly using the VRAM/FLOPs headroom program.md says is a soft constraint, without touching the schedule or attention pattern. This is a single-axis width probe, deliberately separate from I2_depth_sweep_6_10 (which varies DEPTH, i.e. serial capacity) and from D1-throughput's batch-size ideas (which reduce overhead on the SAME small model rather than growing it).
nodes.if_works: val_bpb improves, confirming the model is capacity-constrained rather than purely step-constrained at this budget -- D5's scale-up thesis holds, and other capacity axes (wider MLP ratio, more heads, or combining with a modest depth increase) become high-priority; also implies D1-family throughput micro-optimizations have a lower ceiling than capacity increases.
nodes.if_fails: val_bpb gets worse or unchanged. Check peak_vram_mb and mfu_percent in the run log to distinguish why: if VRAM approaches the ~80GB H100 ceiling, this was a genuine memory-bound tradeoff (capacity costs steps we could not afford). If VRAM stays well under budget but tok/sec drops enough that fewer optimizer steps land in 300s and quality-per-step gains do not cover the deficit, then at THIS token budget (see D4: ~1.5-2.5 corpus passes) the extra parameters simply cannot be trained enough in the available steps -- meaning the run is still in the undertrained-small-model regime and headroom should go to D1-style throughput instead.
nodes.surprise_if: mfu_percent goes UP (not down) despite the wider model -- would mean the champion at dim=512 was overhead-bound rather than FLOPs-bound (matches D3's launch-overhead hypothesis), and widening is actually a free throughput win, not a capacity/steps tradeoff at all.

nodes.title: Shrink WINDOW_PATTERN long-window share (e.g. SSSL -> SSSS, drop the forced full-window last layer) to raise tok/sec
nodes.rationale: Attention FLOPs scale with the effective window; long_window=sequence_len=2048 for L layers vs short_window=1024 for S layers. Removing/shrinking the long-window layers should cut attention cost and raise tok/sec, trading long-range context for more steps in the fixed 300s budget -- a direct test of whether long-range context is worth its throughput cost at this tiny scale.
nodes.if_works: val_bpb improves with higher tok/sec. Supports D1 (throughput-bound) via a different mechanism than batch size, meaning the compute-headroom story is robust to how you recover it, not an artifact of one specific lever.
nodes.if_fails: If tok/sec rises but val_bpb gets worse or flat, long-range context is pulling real weight even at this short horizon and D1 is only partially right -- some per-step quality is load-bearing after all, which argues for future work to preserve or restore long-range capacity while cutting cost elsewhere.

edges.reason: Same claim: model depth/width geometry (DEPTH=8, ASPECT_RATIO=64, HEAD_DIM=128) was inherited from a longer-horizon recipe and never verified against this specific 300s budget. Formed independently before reading D2.

Both are throughput-mechanism diagnoses but locate the overhead in different places: D3 argues GPU-side launch/kernel overhead (grad_accum_steps=2, attention windowing) dominates; D_dataloader argues CPU-side Python document-packing (unoverlapped with GPU compute) dominates. Not mutually exclusive -- both could be true simultaneously and would need separate fixes (I_compile_mode/I_batch_size for D3's mechanism, I_async_loader for this one).

D2-lr-calibration's rationale independently notices the same fact this diagnosis is built on -- 'Muon momentum separately ramps over a hardcoded 300 steps ... independent of TIME_BUDGET' -- as supporting evidence for a broader LR-miscalibration claim (dmodel_lr_scale tuned at 768 applied at 512, no warmup). Convergent observation, but the two diagnoses make different core claims (momentum ramp constant vs LR magnitude/warmup) and have different ideas attached (I_momentum_ramp changes the ramp length; idea-add-warmup and idea-lr-scale-check change LR/warmup) -- independent, not a duplicate.
Same claim: WARMDOWN_RATIO=0.5 is an untested constant, likely inherited from a longer-horizon lineage, that spends half the (very short) budget in LR decay.
Same claim independently stated: fixed wall-clock TIME_BUDGET=300s makes step count (throughput) the dominant lever, per-step quality changes are one-time. Formed before reading D1.

Same claim as D_throughput/D1: MFU/throughput headroom under the fixed 300s budget is the binding constraint. Three agents converged on this independently (D1, D1-throughput, D_throughput) -- strong signal this is the dominant diagnosis, but it is one claim, not three.

Same diff (WARMDOWN_RATIO 0.5 -> 0.2) proposed independently under different diagnosis ids (my D1 vs their D3-warmdown-frac). These collect the same payoff -- one KEEP banks the finding, running the other re-buys it. Theorist should run only one and CUT the other on first result.

Opposite-direction bracket of the same WINDOW_PATTERN knob: mine expands to full context (SSSL->LLLL, betting windowing is pure quality cost with negligible speed benefit at this tiny model), theirs shrinks it further (SSSL->SSSS, betting windowing IS buying real throughput and should be leaned into). Same pattern as the existing idea-warmdown-down/idea-warmdown-up bracket -- a result on one should demote the naive expectation for the other.

Same underlying knob, opposite directions; a result on one is directly informative about the other and both trace to the D3-family launch/overhead-vs-quality question.

Both raise tok/sec but through different parts of the step (device-batch amortization vs CPU/GPU overlap of the dataloader) -- safe to run in parallel, and a result on one does not tell you the sign of the other.

A result on one should trigger review of the other (per HEARTBEAT bracket-relation guidance) rather than being read in isolation -- e.g. if 0.2 improves val_bpb, that raises the prior that 0.7 will hurt it, and vice versa.

both increase model capacity (width vs depth) as a response to unaudited compute headroom, but through different structural levers -- widening changes model_dim/num_heads at fixed depth, the depth sweep changes n_layer at fixed ASPECT_RATIO. They do not share parameters or confound each others measurement, so they can run in the same batch; together they help separate whether headroom is better spent on width or depth.

both spend idle compute headroom but through different mechanisms -- idea-widen-aspect-ratio grows the model (capacity axis, D5), idea-batch256 shrinks per-step overhead on the SAME model size (throughput axis, D1-throughput). Different code paths, no shared parameters touched, safe to batch together; licensing parallelism here is useful because both trace back to unaudited compute headroom and a batch that runs both simultaneously is the fastest way to learn whether headroom should go to capacity or to steps.

both test whether DEPTH=8/ASPECT_RATIO=64 is compute-optimal for the 300s budget -- I_depth_width sweeps DEPTH at fixed ASPECT_RATIO (serial capacity), idea-widen-aspect-ratio sweeps ASPECT_RATIO at fixed DEPTH (per-layer capacity). Same underlying question (model shape optimality under this budget); a result on one should trigger review of the other rather than being read as fully independent evidence.

Opposite-direction bracket of the same WINDOW_PATTERN knob: idea-window-cheap shrinks to all-short (SSSS) betting throughput dominates, I4_window_pattern_LLLL expands to all-long (LLLL) betting quality dominates and windowing barely helps throughput at this scale.
